meta.tagline: The film festival lasts just one week — the real Cannes begins in the other 51

pills: Step one street back from the Croisette
Climb Le Suquet in the early morning

overview.intro: When you hear Cannes, you think red carpet, yacht harbour and film festival. But the city itself goes far beyond all of that. The old town perched on Le Suquet hill, the pine forests of the Lérins Islands, the morning crowds at Forville Market, the shopkeepers of Rue Meynadier — these are the real face of Cannes. The Croisette is the city's most expensive and most touristy facade; one street back, prices drop and the atmosphere changes entirely. Cannes is a small city — everything is walkable, and drinking an espresso while watching the yachts is a French Riviera ritual in its own right.

local_word.definition: Cannes' famous seafront boulevard — 2 kilometres from the yacht harbour to Palm Beach. Luxury hotels, boutiques, sandy beaches and the red carpet during the film festival. Touristy and expensive, but worth walking once. The real tip: right next to the paid private beach concessions on the Croisette there are free public beaches — same sea, half the price.

rules.title: If you're coming during the Film Festival, book well in advance
rules.description: During the Cannes Film Festival, which runs for about two weeks each May, the city fills up completely. Hotel prices triple or quadruple, restaurants are packed, the Croisette is surrounded by barriers. You can't get into the festival itself — accreditation is required. But parallel events and public screenings are free to experience the atmosphere. If you want to come during this period, book at least six months ahead.

rules.title: Step one street back from the Croisette — prices halve
rules.description: Restaurants on or facing the Croisette are two to three times more expensive than the rest of Cannes. The small bistros and cafés on Rue Meynadier, Rue d'Antibes and in Le Suquet neighbourhood are both cheaper and far more local. Go to the Croisette for the view but step one street back for food.

rules.title: Take the early morning ferry to the Lérins Islands
rules.description: Sainte-Marguerite and Saint-Honorat islands are just 15 minutes by ferry from Cannes. In summer the afternoons get very crowded. If you take the 9am or 10am ferry you'll find the islands nearly empty. On Sainte-Marguerite there's the castle where the Man in the Iron Mask was held; on Saint-Honorat, living monks produce their own wine. Separate tickets are needed for each island.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: Train from Nice ~30 min · taxi ~€80 · express bus ~€19.50

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.sub: Single fare €1.80 · day pass €4.60 · contactless card accepted

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.value: French Riviera — 300 sunny days a year
quick_facts.sub: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct ideal · Jul–Aug hot and crowded · Dec–Feb mild

quick_facts.label: Food
quick_facts.value: Socca, pan bagnat, pissaladière, rosé wine

tip.label: Free beach — right next to the Croisette
tip.text: Among the paid private beach concessions stretching along the Croisette, there are free public beaches in front of the Palais des Festivals and at a few other points. Same Mediterranean, same sand, zero cost. If you don't want to rent sunbeds and umbrellas, look for these spots — especially Plage du Midi and Plage de la Bocca, which are quieter and free.

overview.title: Welcome to Cannes

transport.intro: Cannes is small and walkable. Palm Bus is sufficient for getting around the city; trains are faster for neighbouring towns.

items.title: From Nice Airport to Cannes
items.description: Nice Côte d'Azur Airport is the nearest airport to Cannes — about 30 kilometres away. The most practical option: get to Nice-Ville train station, then take the train to Cannes in 30-40 minutes. Express bus (Ligne Azur 210) goes direct from the airport to Cannes train station, about 1 hour, €19.50. Fixed-price taxi around €80. The train-bus combination is both affordable and reasonably fast.

items.title: Train — along the French Riviera
items.description: Cannes train station is in the city centre. 30-40 minutes from Nice, 10 minutes from Antibes, 25 minutes from Grasse. TER regional trains run frequently. Ideal for day trips: Monaco, Antibes, Juan-les-Pins, Nice are all reachable by train. Ticket prices €5-15 depending on the route.

items.title: Palm Bus — city transport
items.description: Cannes' yellow buses cover every point in the city. Single fare €1.80, valid for 74 minutes with free connections within that time. Day pass €4.60. Tickets from the driver or machines at stops. Direct payment by contactless bank card is also possible. Palm Imperial — red open-topped panoramic bus — runs along the Croisette for sightseeing, €1.50 single fare.

items.title: Lérins Islands ferry
items.description: Daily ferry services from the Vieux-Port (old harbour) pier to Sainte-Marguerite and Saint-Honorat islands. Return to Sainte-Marguerite approximately €18, Saint-Honorat separate ticket. Planaria, Trans Côte d'Azur and Riviera Lines are the main operators. Busy in summer — going in the early morning hours is recommended. Fewer sailings in winter, check in advance.

items.title: Walking — the best option
items.description: Cannes centre is compact. From the train station: Forville Market 10 minutes, Le Suquet hilltop 15 minutes, Vieux-Port 10 minutes, the full length of the Croisette 25-30 minutes on foot. The climb to Le Suquet is steep but short. An evening walk along the Croisette is one of Cannes' most classic experiences.

callout.label: Antibes and Juan-les-Pins — easy day trips
callout.text: Antibes is 10 minutes from Cannes by train. Picasso Museum, old city walls and a Provençal market. Juan-les-Pins jazz festival every July. Nice is 30-40 minutes. All reachable by TER regional train, tickets €5-12. For day trip planning, set off from Cannes in the early morning and return in the afternoon.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Location is critical in Cannes — the Croisette is expensive and touristy, Le Suquet has character, the area around the train station is practical.

local_word.definition: Cannes' old neighbourhood, on the hill above Vieux-Port. Narrow stone streets dating from medieval times, the Notre-Dame d'Espérance Church and the city's finest panorama. Away from Cannes' crowds, quiet and local. Nearly empty in the early morning hours. From the top you can see the sea, the yacht harbour and the Estérel mountains all at once.

items.name: Croisette — the seafront boulevard
items.description: One of the world's most famous seafront promenades. Grand hotels, luxury boutiques, private beaches. Everything right in front of you but prices to match. The most expensive and crowded point in the city during the Film Festival. The right place for those who want to experience Cannes at full face value — if the budget allows.

items.name: Le Suquet — old neighbourhood
items.description: Narrow medieval streets, small restaurants and the city's finest views. 5 minutes on foot to Forville Market and Vieux-Port. Away from the Croisette's prices, quiet and authentic. The streets are steep and stepped but worth every step.

items.name: Around the train station
items.description: 10 minutes to the Croisette, 10 minutes to Forville, 10 minutes to Antibes by train. The most central point for transport. Prices lower than the Croisette. Rue d'Antibes shopping street nearby.

items.name: Forville — market neighbourhood
items.description: A small neighbourhood at the foot of Le Suquet, around Forville Market. Comes to life with market activity in the mornings. The pedestrian Rue Meynadier nearby — local bakeries, delis, cheesemongers. The right place to experience Cannes like a local.

items.name: Californie — hilltop neighbourhood
items.description: In the east of the city, on hillside slopes looking out to sea, filled with Belle Époque villa architecture. Reaching the Croisette requires a short walk or bus. A peaceful alternative for longer stays. For those who want to see the Riviera from above.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Cannes can be visited year-round but the Film Festival period is a category apart — come ready for it or plan around it.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The best time
items.description: April is Cannes' most balanced month: temperatures 18-22°C, no crowds, prices reasonable. May is split in two by the Film Festival: quiet and cheap before the festival, the city packed solid during festival week.

callout.label: Cannes Film Festival — when and how
callout.text: Every year in the second half of May, for approximately 12 days. Accreditation is required to get into the festival. But crowds of spectators outside the Palais des Festivals, celebrity-spotting on the Croisette and public screenings are free. If you want to experience the festival atmosphere, you don't need a ticket — just being there is enough.

items.subtitle: Spring · Mimosa blossom, fewer crowds, mild weather

items.label: Summer
items.name: Crowded but lively
items.description: July and August are the French Riviera's most intense period. Cannes beaches are crowded, the Croisette overflows. That said, the sea is at its finest, evenings are long and lively. Early morning hours and after 7pm are more bearable.

callout.label: Plage de la Bocca — escape from the crowds
callout.text: West of Cannes centre, 10 minutes from the train station by bus. Much quieter, more local and a longer stretch of coastline than the central beaches. No paid sunbeds, just sand and sea. On weekday mornings at 9am it's nearly empty. Ideal for escaping Cannes' well-known crowds.

items.subtitle: Summer · Swimming in the Med, packed beaches, nightlife

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Second best time
items.description: September and October are Cannes' most comfortable period. Summer crowds gone, temperatures still 22-25°C, swimming in the Mediterranean still possible. MIPCOM (October) and other professional trade fairs bring life to the city but nowhere near as crowded as the Film Festival. Restaurants and hotels more reasonably priced, the Lérins Islands nearly empty.

callout.label: Lérins Islands — autumn's finest escape
callout.text: In September-October the islands are clear of summer crowds. On Sainte-Marguerite: pine and eucalyptus forests, clear sea, Fort Royal. On Saint-Honorat: an active monastery, vineyards and wine tasting. Allow a full day for both islands — Saint-Honorat's wine is genuinely good.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Summer crowds gone, sea still warm

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet and sunny
items.description: From December to February Cannes quietens. Some restaurants close, beaches are empty but the weather is usually sunny and mild. In January-February mimosa (similar to yellow acacia) blooms in the hills around Grasse and Tanneron — the French Riviera's most breathtaking winter scenery.

callout.label: Mimosa tour — February's secret
callout.text: Every February, the Mimosa Festival in Mandelieu-la-Napoule. Hills covered in yellow flowers, flower gardens grown for perfume. 20-30 minutes from Cannes by car or bus. Perfume museums and factory visits in Grasse are also on this route — one of the most special experiences that brightens the French Riviera in winter.

items.subtitle: Winter · 12-15°C, empty beaches, mimosa season

best_time.title: When to Go

monthly_highlights.text: The Film Festival: world cinema lives here for two weeks — hotels soar, the city crackles; the Cinéma de la Plage screenings are open to all and free.
Festival d'Art Pyrotechnique: the world's best fireworks competition over the bay — the best seat is free, on the sand.
The Yachting Festival: Europe's biggest boat show; the port becomes a floating exhibition of fortunes.
The quiet season: prices drop, the light softens, the Croisette returns to the locals — Cannes at its most sincere.

eat.intro: Cannes is an expensive city — but one street back from the Croisette you eat both better and cheaper.

local_word.definition: The French abbreviation for aperitif culture. Having drinks and nibbles outside before dinner — not just a drink, but the most social moment of the day. On the Riviera: rosé or pastis (anise-flavoured Provençal spirit) with olives, dried fruit and small plates. Between 6pm and 8pm, café terraces fill up for this ritual. When the French sit down for apéro, they don't rush — this time is for nothing else, just this moment.

items.name: Socca
items.description: At the Socca'nne stall in Forville Market, fresh socca cooked over a wood fire. Wrapped in paper, black pepper on top, €3. Eat it hot — when it cools that crispy texture disappears. You can sit at one of the cafés beside the market and ask to bring it in. On the day the market is closed (Monday is the antiques market) there's no socca either.
items.tag: Forville Market, Socca'nne stall · €3 · eat it hot

items.name: Pan bagnat
items.description: The sandwich version of a Niçoise salad — round bread filled with tuna, hard-boiled eggs, tomatoes, peppers, Niçoise olives and anchovies. The lunch dish of the Provençal Riviera. Sold everywhere at kiosks and small shops. How to spot a real pan bagnat: soaked bread, raw vegetables and quality canned tuna. If there are cooked vegetables, it's the wrong version.
items.tag: Kiosks and shops across the city · €5–8

items.name: Pissaladière
items.description: An onion tart — thick pastry base, caramelised onions cooked for hours, Niçoise olives and a lattice of anchovies. At first glance the appearance might suggest pizza, but it's different and far more intense. Fresh from bakeries on Rue Meynadier from the morning. Jean-Luc Pelé is the best on this street. A slice for €2-3, eat it while walking.
items.tag: Rue Meynadier bakeries · Jean-Luc Pelé · €2–3 per slice

items.name: Bouillabaisse
items.description: A rich, saffron-scented broth made from rock fish, served with rouille (garlic mayonnaise) and croutons — a deeply flavourful Riviera soup. Good bouillabaisse in Cannes is expensive: €35-55 per person. Restaurants in Le Suquet neighbourhood are the most reliable. If the menu has no price or it seems very cheap, it's likely a ready-made packet.
items.tag: Le Suquet neighbourhood · €35–55 per person · lunch or dinner

items.name: Rosé wine — Provence style
items.description: Provence produces some of the world's finest rosé. Every bistro and café in Cannes has Provence rosé. A glass of open rosé is €5-8, double on the Croisette. On a warm afternoon, sitting on a café terrace near Forville with this wine is one of the French Riviera's most pure moments.
items.tag: Every bistro and café · €5–8 per glass · away from the Croisette

items.name: Breakfast at Forville Market
items.description: The covered market open from 7am to 1pm. Mondays are the antiques market, all other days food. Fresh fruit, vegetables, cheese, fish, flowers and local products. Picking up socca, fougasse (Provençal olive bread) and fresh cheese and sitting outside is both cheap and the most local Cannes breakfast you can have. Chefs and grandmothers are at their most animated between 8am and 10am.

callout.label: Rue Meynadier — Cannes' local street
callout.text: A pedestrian street running from Forville Market to Rue d'Antibes. Bakeries, cheesemongers, delis, confectionery shops. The real Cannes shopkeepers are here, in contrast to the Croisette's luxury windows. Ideal for picking up a picnic — fresh bread, cheese and a bottle of rosé and you're ready for the beach. Most lively between 8am and 10am.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Cannes' finest corners are one step away from the Croisette or a few metres higher up.

items.name: Le Suquet hilltop — Notre-Dame d'Espérance
items.description: Climb the steps from Vieux-Port and you reach the top of Le Suquet. From in front of Notre-Dame d'Espérance Church you can see the yacht harbour, the Croisette and the Estérel mountains. Go 30 minutes before sunset — the light hits this hill directly. Bring a bottle of rosé and sit on the terrace. A tenth of the Croisette's crowds, free and far more beautiful.
items.rarity: Right above the Croisette — a viewpoint with no crowds

items.name: Île Sainte-Marguerite
items.description: 15 minutes by ferry from Vieux-Port. At Fort Royal you can see the cell where the Man in the Iron Mask was held — whether fact or legend is debated, but the cell itself is real. The rest of the island is pine and eucalyptus forest, clear sea coves and walking trails. Even in midsummer it stays peaceful. Have lunch on the island — the restaurant is simple but the fish is fresh.
items.rarity: The island where the Man in the Iron Mask was held — 15 minutes across

items.name: Île Saint-Honorat
items.description: The smaller island next to Sainte-Marguerite, reached by a separate ferry. An active monastery since the 5th century — monks still live here today and tend their vines. The monastery wine is world-renowned; tastings and sales are available to visitors. The island is small, walkable in its entirety. Can be visited on the same day as Sainte-Marguerite — buy separate tickets for each island.
items.rarity: A living monastery, vineyards and its own wine

items.name: Vallauris — Picasso's pottery village
items.description: 20 minutes from Cannes by bus. Picasso lived here between 1948 and 1955 and discovered the art of ceramics here. Active pottery workshops and small galleries still exist today. Musée National Picasso La Guerre et la Paix — a chapel that Picasso personally painted and donated to the town. Ticketed but affordable, not crowded, genuinely impressive.
items.rarity: Cannes' Picasso connection — just outside the city

items.name: Grasse — perfume city
items.description: 25-30 minutes from Cannes by train or bus. The world's perfume capital — the raw materials for Chanel No.5 come from here. Fragonard, Molinard and Galimard perfume factories offer free tours; workshop sessions are ticketed. The old town has narrow streets and Provençal breakfast spots. In February-March mimosa blooms along the roads.
items.rarity: Mimosa and the perfume capital — right behind Cannes

items.name: Forville antiques market
items.description: Every Monday Forville Market transforms from food into an antiques, vintage and second-hand market. Old photographs, frames, jewellery, books, plates. Prices far lower than auction houses. The best finds when stalls are being set up at 7am. Sellers are generally open to bargaining. A completely different and far more authentic Cannes experience, in contrast to the Croisette's glamour.

callout.label: Chemin des Étoiles — handprints of cinema stars
callout.text: In front of the Palais des Festivals, a walkway reminiscent of Hollywood's Walk of Fame but far more modest. The hand and footprints of stars who've attended the film festival are pressed into concrete blocks. Free, open 24/7. Lit up at night — ideal for stopping on an evening walk. Climbing the red-carpeted steps of the Palais des Festivals is also free and perfect for photos.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Eat socca at Forville — fresh in the morning
items.sub: Forville Market, Socca'nne stall. Every day except Monday, 7am-1pm. €3. Eat it hot — the taste goes when it cools.

items.label: Climb Le Suquet — at sunset
items.sub: Steps from Vieux-Port. Panorama from in front of Notre-Dame d'Espérance. Arrive 30 minutes before sunset. Free.

items.label: Take the ferry to the Lérins Islands
items.sub: Vieux-Port pier. Go on the first morning sailing — crowded in the afternoon. Sainte-Marguerite and Saint-Honorat are separate tickets.

items.label: Buy pissaladière on Rue Meynadier
items.sub: Pedestrian street, near Forville. Fresh slice from the bakery, €2-3. Freshest between 8am and 10am.

items.label: Take an evening walk along the Croisette
items.sub: From Palais des Festivals to Palm Beach. 2km. Most beautiful after sunset. Yachts, lights, the Estérel silhouette.

items.label: Visit Chemin des Étoiles
items.sub: In front of Palais des Festivals. Stars' handprints. Free. Take a photo on the red-carpeted steps.

items.label: Go to Forville Market in the early morning
items.sub: Every day except Monday, 7am-1pm. Fresh fish, cheese, vegetables, socca. Best hours 8am-10am.

items.label: Go on a perfume tour to Grasse
items.sub: 25-30 minutes by train or bus from Cannes. Fragonard or Molinard factory — free tour. Make your own perfume (ticketed).

items.label: Drink Provence rosé — away from the Croisette
items.sub: Cafés around Le Suquet or Forville. A glass €5-8. Double the price on the Croisette.

items.label: Try pan bagnat
items.sub: Kiosks and shops across the city. Niçoise tuna sandwich. €5-8. The real thing: soaked bread, raw vegetables.

items.label: Go to the Forville antiques market
items.sub: Mondays only. 7am-1pm. Vintage items, old photographs, jewellery. Bargain.

items.label: Visit the Picasso chapel in Vallauris
items.sub: 20 minutes from Cannes by bus. Musée National Picasso La Guerre et la Paix. Ticketed but affordable. Not crowded.

checklist.title: Cannes Checklist
checklist.completion_message: Cannes charmed you without the red carpet — come back slower next time.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Cannes belongs to the stars for two weeks a year — and to smart travellers for the other fifty. Know these four and live it without paying red-carpet prices.

items.name: A 'view' coffee on the Croisette terraces
items.description: Espresso on the palm-lined boulevard sells at several times the price; you're paying not for coffee but for the right to watch Bentleys pass.
items.instead: Drink your coffee around the Forville market or on Rue Meynadier; live the Croisette for free, on foot.

items.name: 'Party ticket' sellers during the Festival
items.description: Most 'starry gala' tickets sold on the street and online in May are fake; real invitations are never for sale.
items.instead: Soak up the festival around the Palais and at the public beach screenings (Cinéma de la Plage — free).

items.name: The beach club sunbed bill
items.description: On the Croisette's private beaches, a sunbed and umbrella easily reach dinner-budget territory.
items.instead: Use the public beaches: Plage du Midi and the public stretches by the Palais offer the same sand for free.

items.name: Haggling for a 'celebrity villas boat tour'
items.description: The pricey 'celebrity tour' sold at the port mostly amounts to pointing at walls from a distance.
items.instead: Spend the same money on the Lérins Islands ferry: Sainte-Marguerite's forest and the Man in the Iron Mask's cell tell a real story.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: The Cannes equation is simple: the first street along the sea is the show, the second street is the city. If a price tag hurts, climb one street up.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Market, old hill and an island escape

steps.title: Breakfast at Forville market
steps.description: Fruit from the stalls, something from the bakery, espresso standing up; Cannes without make-up lives under this roof.

steps.title: Climb Le Suquet
steps.description: Up the old quarter's narrow lanes to Notre-Dame d'Espérance: the bay, the islands and the tiled roofs at your feet.

steps.title: Ferry to Île Sainte-Marguerite
steps.description: Walk the pine and eucalyptus forest, see the fort of the Man in the Iron Mask; the paths drop to the sea.

steps.title: The Croisette walk
steps.description: Back on shore, walk the boulevard end to end: the Palais steps, the handprints, the beaches. Watching is free.

steps.title: Rue d'Antibes + Meynadier
steps.description: Windows and boutiques; shop here for the evening's cheese, wine and tarte.

steps.title: Dinner in Le Suquet
steps.description: Fish or bouillabaisse at the small restaurants on the hillside; the harbour lights below.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The Cannes classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: market, Suquet, island, Croisette.

steps.title: The quiet island of Lérins
steps.description: Morning ferry to Saint-Honorat: the monks' monastery, vineyards and a wine tasting; swim in the island coves, fish at the harbour at night.

steps.title: Perfume and ceramics
steps.description: A perfume workshop in Grasse in the morning (make your own scent), Picasso's pottery traces in Vallauris in the afternoon, a farewell rosé in Cannes at night.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Riviera French begins with courtesy; these five open every door.

items.meaning: Hello — the mandatory first word of every exchange
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — rosé glasses rise to this
It's magnificent! — you'll need it looking over the bay from Le Suquet
